# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>

# Review: *Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem* (Varga & Holm, Comment)

This comment does valuable forensic work. Using the microdata, it documents several things the original working paper hid or got wrong:
- **Attrition:** seven of the nine withdrawals happened after the reduced schedule began, which contradicts the working paper.
- **Output measure:** managers' ratings ran systematically above what their own records showed (19 of 23 organisations).
- **Hours:** actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%.
- **Revenue:** in real terms it fell, rather than rising.

The corrections in Sections 1–5 are largely sound. They confirm several concerns I raised about the Halden paper: survivor bias, inflation, and the per-hour metric guaranteeing gains in every sector.

The problem is the leap from those corrections to the headline conclusion. "Entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty" is not supported by the comment's own numbers. It also conflicts with the randomised evidence the comment cites, which it cites selectively.

The arithmetic checks out:
- 95.1/0.8 = +18.9%; 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%; 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%.
- Hours ratios: 34.6/40.3 = 0.859; 34.8/40.4 = 0.861.
- Real revenue: 1.014/1.041 = −2.6%.

The one exception is the hours decomposition (§2.4 below).

---

## 1. The central conclusion overreaches (most important)

### 1.1 The comment's own best estimate is a gain
- **The fully corrected figure is +10.8%,** using record-based output and actual hours.
- **The corrections account for about half of the reported gain:** (23.4 − 10.8)/23.4 ≈ 54%. That fits the abstract's "most," but not the conclusion's "entirely."
- **Novelty is what closes the rest of the gap,** and it is argued, not measured (see 1.3).

### 1.2 The randomised evidence is cited selectively
- **Section 5 calls Varden's counter stratum (−11.4% output per employee) "the most reliable finding in the literature."** But the same trial, with the same design, reports:
  - **+12.5% output per actual hour in case-processing** (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4);
  - **+6.7% per actual hour even in the counter stratum.**
- **Varden already meets the comment's own recommended standards:** record-based output, actual hours from timesheets, randomisation, and no reliance on volunteering organisations.
- **The two estimates line up.** The comment's corrected Halden figure (+10.8%) is close to Varden's case-processing estimate (+12.5%). Two independent studies, with very different designs, converging on a gain of roughly 10–12% per actual hour is evidence *for* a real per-hour effect, not against it.

The comment should engage with this directly. As written, it treats Varden as authoritative where it supports a negative finding and doesn't mention it where it doesn't.

### 1.3 The novelty argument rests on weak evidence
- **Energy is not output.** A decline in self-reported energy does not show that per-hour output declined.
- **Two points cannot support a trend.** Drawing a straight line through month 3 (+0.61 SD) and month 6 (+0.29 SD) to reach "baseline at around month ten" assumes a functional form the data can't support. Energy could level off well above zero.
- **The microdata can test this directly.** The Halden output index was collected *monthly*. If novelty drives the result, record-based output per actual hour should decline across months 1–6 in the 17-organisation subset. The comment should report that trajectory rather than infer novelty from a survey measure.
- **Varden partly speaks to this.** Its gains are measured at nine months, against a control group. That doesn't rule out novelty (staff knew their assignment), but it is longer than six months and closer to the comment's own threshold.
- **The burden of proof works both ways.** "Six months cannot distinguish novelty from a durable effect" supports "not established," not "entirely an artifact." The defensible conclusion is uncertainty about persistence, not a finding of zero.

### 1.4 The abstract and conclusion disagree
- **The abstract says the four problems "account for most of the reported gain."** The conclusion says the gains are "entirely an artifact."
- **The four problems don't map onto the corrections.** Revenue (problem 4) has no bearing on the per-hour estimate. Attrition (problem 1) is never corrected in Table 2 (see 2.1).

## 2. Methodological issues in the re-analysis

### 2.1 Attrition is documented but not corrected
- **The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems gives 10.8%.** But the 17 organisations in that estimate are all survivors among the 61. No adjustment for the nine withdrawals is applied.
- **The 10.8% therefore still carries survivor bias.** That would lower it further, but the comment should quantify this, not just assert it.
- **Suggestion:** bound the effect on all 70 enrolled organisations. For example, assign withdrawn organisations an output of 80, meaning no per-hour gain, or use the output records they held before withdrawing, if any exist. Then report the 70-organisation estimate under those assumptions.

### 2.2 Table 2 compares different samples
- **Each row uses a different subset** (61, 23, 27, 17 organisations). Differences between rows mix the effect of each correction with differences in which organisations are included.
- **A cleaner decomposition would apply all four specifications within the 17-organisation subset.** That needs the manager-reported index for those 17 alongside the record-based figure (95.4) and actual hours (0.861).
- **No uncertainty is reported.** The comment demands rigour of the original but gives no CI for +10.8%. With 17 organisations the interval is probably wide.
- **The weighting is unstated.** It isn't clear whether the corrected estimates are employee-weighted, as the original's were. If they're not, they aren't directly comparable with 23.4%.

### 2.3 Some "records" measure input, not output
- **Billable hours delivered** is listed as a record-based output measure. In professional services, billable hours fall mechanically when working hours fall, so the measure partly tracks hours rather than output.
- **For organisations using this measure, the record-based index understates output,** and the manager–record gap may partly reflect managers reasonably discounting a flawed metric.
- **Suggestion:** report Table 1 separately by type of record, or drop billable-hours organisations as a robustness check.

### 2.4 The hours decomposition doesn't add up
- **The comment attributes the shortfall to two sources:** longer remaining days (+0.7 h/day) and work on the day off (1.6 h/week).
- **Applied to the baseline, these imply far more hours than reported:**
  - Baseline: 40.3 h ÷ 5 days = 8.06 h/day.
  - Pilot: 4 × (8.06 + 0.7) + 1.6 ≈ 36.6 h/week.
  - Reported: 34.6 h/week.
- **Working backwards from 34.6 h:** (34.6 − 1.6) ÷ 4 = 8.25 h/day, an increase of about 0.2 h/day, not 0.7.

The authors should check whether the +0.7 is measured against scheduled hours, not baseline actual hours, or whether another figure is wrong.

### 2.5 Small subsets behind sector claims
- **The retail and hospitality record-based figure (−11.2%) rests on three organisations.** The direction is plausible, but the comment should flag the sample size.
- **The data note caveat about non-random subsets is good, but it appears only at the end.** Organisations with time tracking and submitted records may be systematically different, more measurement-oriented for instance, and the direction of that bias is unclear. The caveat belongs in the abstract and conclusion too.

## 3. The Varden meetings analysis is mischaracterised

The comment says the meetings correlation was "selected for analysis after the results were known" and that it "should not be cited as a mechanism."

- **The timing is wrong as described.** Varden reports collecting the meeting data in month six, at managers' request. That is before the nine-month results existed, not after them.
- **Varden didn't claim it as a mechanism.** The trial authors explicitly flagged the analysis as unregistered, said a seven-office correlation "cannot establish a mechanism," and pre-registered a confirmatory test.
- **There is independent support.** Halden's manager interviews (47 of 58 mentioning meeting cuts) point the same way, though also anecdotally.
- **It cuts against the comment's own conclusion.** If meeting reductions do explain part of the gain, that is a real change in how work is organised. It is not an artifact of measurement, selection or novelty. It may be achievable without cutting hours, which is a fair policy point. But it is not consistent with "entirely an artifact."

"Not yet established; awaiting the registered test" is accurate. "Should not be cited" goes further than the evidence warrants.

## 4. Smaller points

- **Deflator.** CPI is a rough deflator for organisational revenue. Sector-specific output price indices would be better, though the qualitative point (real revenue probably fell) likely holds.
- **19 of 23.** This is strong evidence of a systematic manager–record gap (a sign test gives p ≈ 0.003). Saying so would strengthen §2.
- **Tone.** The "no bad faith" framing in §2 is fair and well judged. The same even-handedness should apply to the Varden authors in §7.
- **Recommendations.** The closing recommendations are sound: record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, at least 18 months of follow-up, and intention-to-treat including withdrawals. Varden already meets most of them.

---

## What the evidence supports

A conclusion consistent with this comment's own analysis and the randomised evidence would be:

> The Halden pilot substantially overstated the per-hour gain. Correcting for manager-reported output and scheduled hours roughly halves it, to about 11% in the subset where correction is possible, and unaddressed survivor bias would reduce it further. This corrected figure is close to the ~12% per-actual-hour gain found in the randomised Varden trial's case-processing offices. Where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output per employee and service, even when per-hour output rises. Whether per-hour gains persist beyond six to nine months is not yet established.

## Highest-value revisions

1. Replace "entirely an artifact" with a conclusion matching the estimates. Engage with Varden's case-processing result.
2. Test the novelty hypothesis using the monthly output data, not the energy trajectory.
3. Apply an attrition correction or bounds, and report the estimate for all 70 enrolled organisations.
4. Run all specifications within one subset, with CIs and the weighting stated.
5. Reconcile the hours decomposition (+0.7 h/day vs about +0.2 h/day implied).
6. Correct the characterisation of the Varden meetings analysis.
